title: How to compare agroforestry scenarios before implementation
excerpt: A practical framework for comparing site conditions, species choices, management assumptions and long-term project scenarios.
sections: Start with the decision
Define the choice the team needs to make. A useful comparison is specific about location, project boundary, time horizon and the alternatives under review.
Keep assumptions visible
Record the climate, soil, species, management, labour and price assumptions used in each scenario. Visible assumptions make differences easier to discuss and revise.
Compare more than one outcome
Review production, carbon, water, soil, labour and economics together where relevant. A scenario that improves one indicator may introduce a trade-off elsewhere.
Use projections as decision support
Modelled results are not guarantees. Treat them as structured evidence for field validation, specialist review and better-informed planning.

title: What an agroforestry investment plan should make clear
excerpt: The essential questions an agroforestry investment plan should answer for project teams, funders and delivery partners.
sections: What is being implemented?
Describe the site, intended land-use system, species mix, management approach and delivery responsibilities in terms that each stakeholder can understand.
Which assumptions drive the plan?
Make biological, operational and financial assumptions explicit. This helps reviewers distinguish known inputs from projections and uncertainties.
How will progress be reviewed?
Connect the plan to practical monitoring questions, data ownership and review points. Keep modelling, measurement and independent verification clearly separated.
Where are the trade-offs?
Explain how alternative designs affect farmer value, programme cost, environmental outcomes and timing. A useful plan supports a decision rather than hiding uncertainty.

title: From site data to agroforestry monitoring and reporting
excerpt: How project teams can connect baseline information and scenario assumptions to a coherent monitoring and reporting approach.
sections: Build a usable baseline
Start with the location, current land use, inventory, management context and data quality. Document gaps instead of filling them with unsupported precision.
Connect design and monitoring
Choose indicators that relate to the project decisions and assumptions. Monitoring becomes more useful when teams know which question each data point helps answer.
Separate measured and modelled information
Label observed data, calculated values and forward-looking projections clearly. This distinction helps readers interpret results and limits overclaiming.
Keep the reporting trail reviewable
Retain source notes, model versions, scenario definitions and decision records so results can be revisited as field information improves.
